doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Louis Jordan's advice, Columbus, the group's end and rejoining Louis in 1966
summary: The Columbus run, the group's decline, Marty quitting Louis for his children, and returning in 1966 for Jones Beach.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: to Columbus we’re leaving tomorrow night after the gig.” He says, “You’re leaving after the gig? You’re going to drive” We says, “Yeah.” He says, “Let me give you a little clue. Don’t drive more than 200 miles, I don’t care how cold it is, without getting out the car and running around the car ten times.” We said, “What?” “Trust me.” I think he saved our lives. Because we did it, we listened to him. Because we had two cars, we were caravan style. And we went a couple of hundred miles, we stopped, got out of the car, [breathes] ready. So that’s what we did. So Louis Jordan saved our lives. And then we went to Columbus, Ohio, and we played there for about four weeks and it was freezing. Man we had snow and sleet and ice. And Teddy and I had a suite of rooms there and we put the T.V. on just while we were getting dressed to go to work, and the guy would say, if you don’t have business out there, don’t go out tonight, stay home. This guy was ruining our business — shut up. We’d go to work the place would be packed. Packed. We packed the room every night. They loved it. It was great. Because we had two grand pianos, and we used to play and then we would sing like [sings] “Straighten Up and Fly Right.” And then we’d play fours, like I’d play then he’d play then we’d do fours. Then we would scat fours across the piano, and the bass and drum are playing [scats]. Man I’ll tell you I loved it. I’m so disappointed that we didn’t continue on and do better with that group, because after that we went to Chicago and it was a bad, bad, bad booking, because they booked us in there Easter week and we had absolutely no business at all in the place, no business. So that was like our demise. From there on it was downhill all the way. And then after that — that was ’55, in ’66 I went back with Louis. And the funny thing is by that time, when I was with Louis when my kids were little, I used to call my wife twice a week. Every Thursday night and every Sunday morning. Thursday night I talked to my wife and Sunday morning because I could talk to the kids. And they used to cry and cry, they didn’t want to talk to me, and finally my daughter didn’t want to talk. I said why is she crying? She says everybody has a daddy but me. Oh man it broke my heart. And then Thursday night I talked to her, I said, “Daddy’s going to make some money, I want to buy you some—” I don’t want —” Okay I finally convinced her that everything was okay, I said, “put your brother on.” She said, “he doesn’t want to talk to you.” He was two years old. “He don’t want to talk to you either, he’s crying.” So I said that’s it. I went to the manager, I called him, I said, “Frenchie, I’m giving my notice.” I quit the band

see? So now in ’66, Glaser calls me again because — what happened? Oh he said, “we’re going into Jones Beach.” That’s what made me go back with the band. They were going to Jones Beach in New York for the summer. Because Guy Lombardo used to put a show out there every year for the whole summer, So that convinced me to say okay. And I did, I went back in ’66. And it’s too long a story. But what else have you got to do?
